To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
P. aeruginosa produces alginate as a component of biofilm architecture and that alginate biosynthesis is upregulated in biofilms compared with planktonically grown cells.
alginate biosynthetic genes are activated by substratum in P. aeruginosa biofilms.
the algC promoter was upregulated in biofilms compared to planktonic cells and was activated by substrata.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the expression of the alginate gene during the formation of a biofilm by P. aeruginosa.
the role of the substratum in the expression of alginate genes in the biofilm state and with the role of algC in biofilm development.
the expression of the P. aeruginosa algC promoter in a biofilm environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
biofilms of P. aeruginosa are capable of producing alginate.
biofilm formation induces algC expression and alginate synthesis by Pseudomonus aeruginosa.
the alginate promoter is active in biofilms and that the alginate gene is induced by the substratum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alginate biosynthetic gene expression is activated in biofilms.
biofilm cells are capable of expressing algC and alginate biosynthetic enzymes at levels that exceed those of planktonic cells.
alginate production by Pseudomonos aeruginosa is upregulated when the organism is grown as a biofilms on a substratum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biofilm cells have a greater capacity to produce alginate than planktonic cells and that the alginate gene expression in biofilm cells is regulated differently from that in planktonic cells.
alginate gene expression in biofilm cells is activated in response to the substratum.
the alginate promoter is active in biofilms, which may be a key step in the development of chronic infections by P. aeruginosa.
